valueChain.summary: Airlines sell a perishable product (a seat on a given flight) using aircraft and fuel paid for in dollars, and fares are reset daily against rivals, so a typical airline keeps only a few per cent of revenue as profit. Much of the money in the chain is made around the airline: by lessors, engine makers and MRO shops upstream, regulated airports in the middle, and distribution platforms and loyalty programmes downstream.

stages.name: Aircraft, engines and leasing
activities: Design, certify and build airframes and engines
Finance aircraft through operating leases and sale-and-leaseback
Sell spare parts and long-term engine service contracts
revenueDrivers: Engine aftermarket (parts, shop visits) over a 20 to 25 year engine life
Lease rentals set by aircraft value and lease rate factor
costDrivers: R&D and certification of new models
Supply chain for engines, castings and avionics

kpis.name: Lease rate factor
kpis.formula: monthly lease rental / aircraft market value
kpis.benchmark: approx. 0.65-0.85% a month for new narrowbodies, rising with interest rates

kpis.name: Order backlog cover
kpis.benchmark: approx. 10 years or more for current narrowbody families

stages.marginNote: Strong: the engine aftermarket and leasing earn well above airlines. Large lessors run operating EBITDA of roughly 85% of lease revenue (much lower net after depreciation and interest); airframe makers earn mid to high single-digit operating margins on commercial aircraft (approx.).

stages.name: Maintenance and engine overhaul (MRO)
revenueDrivers: Fleet size, age and flight hours
Engine shop visits (the largest single maintenance events)
Power-by-the-hour contracts priced per flight hour

kpis.name: Technical dispatch reliability
kpis.formula: flights departing without a technical delay / scheduled flights
kpis.benchmark: approx. 99.5% or better for a well-run narrowbody fleet

kpis.name: Engine shop visit turnaround
kpis.formula: days from engine removal to return to service
kpis.benchmark: approx. 60-90 days normally; far longer during parts shortages

stages.marginNote: Moderate to good: roughly 10-15% EBITDA for independent MROs (approx.), higher on engine work controlled by the engine makers.

stages.name: Airports, fuel and ground services
activities: Runways, terminals and air traffic control
Ground handling: check-in, baggage, ramp, pushback
players: Oil marketing companies and fuel farms
revenueDrivers: Aeronautical charges (landing, parking, user development fees) set by regulators
Non-aeronautical income: retail, duty free, car parks, real estate

kpis.name: Aircraft turnaround time
kpis.benchmark: approx. 25-35 minutes for a low-cost narrowbody turn

stages.marginNote: Split: large airports earn high EBITDA (often 50%+) under regulated returns; ground handlers are labour-heavy with thin single-digit to low double-digit EBITDA (approx.).

stages.name: Airline network and flight operations
activities: Flying the schedule: crew, fuel, dispatch, disruption recovery
costDrivers: Fuel (approx. 30-40% of costs for Indian airlines)

kpis.name: Load factor
kpis.formula: revenue passenger km (RPK) / available seat km (ASK)

kpis.name: Unit margin
kpis.formula: RASK - CASK (operating revenue minus operating cost, per ASK)
kpis.benchmark: approx. ₹0.2-0.6 per ASK in a good year for Indian airlines; negative in downturns

stages.marginNote: Thin and volatile: global airline net margins of about 2-4% in good years (approx.) and deep losses in downturns.

stages.name: Distribution and booking
activities: Distributing fares and seats to agents (GDS, NDC connections)
revenueDrivers: GDS fees per booked flight segment
OTA commissions, incentives and convenience fees

kpis.name: Direct booking share
kpis.formula: bookings through the airline's own channels / total bookings

stages.marginNote: Attractive at scale but uneven: the largest GDS group earns EBITDA of about 35-40%, smaller rivals nearer 15-20% (approx.); Indian OTAs earn thin take rates on flights (low to mid single digits of booking value) and more on hotels.

stages.name: Loyalty, ancillaries and the traveller
activities: Selling add-ons: bags, seats, meals, upgrades
Running loyalty programmes and co-brand cards
Serving the traveller through disruptions, refunds and complaints
revenueDrivers: Points sold to banks and partners
costDrivers: Cost of seats given for redemptions

kpis.name: Ancillary revenue per passenger
kpis.benchmark: approx. ₹500-700 for Indian low-cost airlines (reported non-ticket revenue, which can include some cargo); about €20-50 at European low-cost and ultra-low-cost airlines

kpis.name: Points breakage
kpis.formula: points expected never to be redeemed / points issued

stages.marginNote: High: loyalty programmes often earn 30-50%+ margins on points sold to partners (approx.), which is why some have been valued above their parent airline.

valueChain.profitPools: Over a cycle, airlines earn below their cost of capital, while lessors, engine makers (through the aftermarket), large airports, GDSs and loyalty programmes earn above it. Those stages own scarce or locked-in assets: certified designs and installed engine fleets, airport monopolies with regulated returns, two-sided booking networks, and loyalty currencies that banks must buy. Airlines compete in a fragmented, price-transparent market with perishable inventory, so most cost savings are passed on to travellers as lower fares.

unitEconomics.unit: per passenger, Indian domestic low-cost sector of about 1,100 km (approximate)

lines.item: Base fare (excluding taxes and airport fees passed through)

unitEconomics.result: Operating profit per passenger ≈ ₹400 (about 7% of ₹5,800 revenue); a 5% rise in fuel cost wipes out over a quarter of it

valueChain.india: Two airline groups carry roughly 90% of domestic passengers, slots at metro airports are scarce, and new entrants have a long record of failure. Jet fuel sits outside GST and carries state VAT (high in several states, though some cut it temporarily during the 2026 fuel price spike), which helps make fuel about 30-40% of airline costs, and most aircraft are leased in dollars, so rupee weakness raises costs directly. DGCA regulates safety, AERA sets charges at major airports, the UDAN scheme subsidises regional routes, and since 2025 India has given the Cape Town Convention the force of law, which strengthens lessors' repossession rights and should lower leasing costs.

workedExample.problem: An Indian low-cost airline's operating margin fell 3 points even though load factor and yield were flat
trace: Start at the airline (s4): revenue per ASK is flat, so the fall must be in cost per ASK, which rose about 3%.

Fuel, crew and airport costs per ASK are flat; the rise sits in aircraft ownership and maintenance per ASK, which together rose about 12% (about ₹175 on a ₹5,400 cost base per passenger, or 3 points of margin).

Trace ownership upstream to s1: several aircraft are grounded waiting for engines, yet their rent is still payable, and the airline has taken short-term replacement aircraft to protect the schedule, so it pays twice for the same ASKs.
Trace maintenance to s2: engine shop visits that took about 75 days now take over 200 because overhaul shops are short of parts, and the airline pays for spare and short-term leased engines.
Root cause: an engine durability and parts problem two stages upstream, not anything the airline changed in its own operation.
workedExample.lesson: When an airline cost line moves, follow it to the stage that controls it; many airline problems start with suppliers the airline cannot manage directly.

cases.title: Domestic LCC profit halves despite growth
cases.prompt: Our client is a mid-sized Indian low-cost airline that flies only domestic routes. Last year its revenue grew 9% to about ₹12,000 crore, but operating profit halved from ₹1,400 crore to ₹700 crore. The CEO wants to know why profit fell and what to do about it.
clarifyingFacts: Q: Did capacity change? A: Yes. The airline added 12 aircraft and grew available seat kilometres (ASKs) by 15%.
Q: What happened to load factor and fares? A: Load factor fell from 88% to 84%; the average fare per passenger was roughly flat.
Q: Did fuel prices move? A: Jet fuel prices were roughly flat in rupees, and fuel burned per ASK did not change.
Q: Anything else new? A: The new aircraft came on sale-and-leaseback deals at higher rentals, and most new routes link Tier-2 cities.

modelTree.label: Why did operating profit halve to ₹700 crore despite 9% revenue growth?

children.label: Revenue: why only +9% when capacity grew 15%?
Rentals and depreciation on existing fleet
Airport, navigation and ground handling charges

hypotheses: Capacity on new Tier-2 routes ran ahead of demand: the 4-point fall in load factor (88% to 84%) alone cuts passenger revenue growth from about 15% to about 10%.
Higher rentals on the new sale-and-leaseback aircraft pushed aircraft ownership cost per ASK up while fuel per ASK stayed flat.
hints: Use the profit identity, but judge each side against the growth in capacity rather than in absolute terms.
Level 1: revenue, judged against 15% more capacity, and costs, judged against the same 15%.
Fuel: jet fuel price per litre and litres burned per ASK. Both are flat here, so fuel grew in line with capacity and can be set aside.

keyMetrics.name: Revenue per ASK (RASK)
keyMetrics.formula: total revenue / available seat kilometres

keyMetrics.name: Cost per ASK (CASK)
keyMetrics.formula: total operating cost / available seat kilometres

keyMetrics.name: Load factor
keyMetrics.formula: revenue passenger kilometres / available seat kilometres

commonMistakes: Treating 9% revenue growth as good news and jumping to cost cuts, when revenue per ASK actually fell about 5% because capacity outgrew demand.
Comparing costs in absolute terms; costs were bound to rise with 15% more flying, so the useful question is cost per ASK.

frameworkPick.why: The question is why operating profit fell, so decompose profit into revenue and cost drivers and compare each with capacity growth.

distractorWhyNot.growth: The airline is already growing fast; the problem is that growth diluted profit.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Operating efficiency is one possible cost driver inside the profit tree, not the overall frame.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: Profit halved but the airline is still profitable and has no cash crisis; a turnaround frame jumps to rescue actions before diagnosing why profit fell.

cases.title: Size paid seat selection in India
cases.prompt: An Indian low-cost airline is deciding how much to invest in a new seat-merchandising tool and wants to know how big the paid seat selection market is. India flies about 165 million domestic passengers a year. How big is the annual revenue pool for paid seat selection across all domestic airlines?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Do seats included free in bundled or business fares count? A: No, only seats a passenger pays for separately.
Q: What passenger mix should I assume? A: Roughly 35% business travellers, 30% leisure solo travellers or couples, 35% families and groups.
Q: What does a paid seat cost? A: Between ₹200 and ₹1,500 depending on the row; front rows and extra legroom are at the top end.
Q: What time frame and currency? A: One year, today's market, in rupees.

modelTree.label: Annual paid seat-selection revenue on Indian domestic flights (₹ crore)

children.label: Share buying a paid seat: ~25% (aisle, front rows)
Share buying a paid seat: ~35% (to sit together)

hypotheses: The total pool is about ₹1,700 crore a year (business ~₹870 crore, families ~₹710 crore, solo leisure ~₹150 crore).
Business travellers and families make up over 90% of the pool, so the tool should prioritise front-row and 'sit together' offers.
Each 1-point rise in industry attach rate is worth roughly ₹70 crore a year at today's average paid-seat price of about ₹435.
hints: Segment passengers by why they would pay for a seat, because attach rates differ a lot between segments.
Level 1: business travellers; leisure solo travellers and couples; families and groups.
Solo leisure and couples: 30% of 165m ≈ 50m passengers x ~10% buying x ~₹300 ≈ ₹150 crore.

keyMetrics.name: Seat revenue pool
keyMetrics.formula: sum over segments of (passengers x attach rate x average paid-seat price)

keyMetrics.name: Attach rate
keyMetrics.formula: paid seats sold / passengers flown

commonMistakes: Applying one attach rate to all 165 million passengers, when families and business travellers buy at roughly three times the rate of solo leisure travellers.
Counting seats included in bundled fares or business cabins, which no airline can sell separately.

frameworkPick.why: The question asks how big a revenue pool is, so build an estimate from passengers, attach rate and price.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: No seat price is being set; current prices are only an input to the estimate.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Segments are a tool inside the estimate, not the question being asked.
distractorWhyNot.growth: The client is not yet asking how to grow its seat revenue, only how big the pool is.

cases.title: Should an OTA drop its convenience fee?
cases.prompt: Our client is an Indian online travel agency that sells about 12 million domestic flight bookings a year. It charges a ₹350 convenience fee per booking, and a rival has just made flight bookings fee-free. Should our client drop its fee too?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does the OTA earn per booking apart from the fee? A: About ₹250 from airline commissions and GDS incentives; variable costs (payment gateway, customer support) are about ₹150 per booking.
Q: Has volume fallen since the rival's move? A: Bookings are down about 5% in the six weeks since.
Q: Does the OTA sell anything else to flight customers? A: About 8% of flight customers also book a hotel, worth roughly ₹900 contribution per hotel booking.
Q: What is the objective? A: Protect contribution from domestic flights, currently about ₹540 crore a year.

modelTree.label: Should the OTA drop its ₹350 fee on domestic flight bookings?

children.label: Contribution if we drop the fee
Bookings won back from the rival
New flyers attracted by a lower total price
Flight contribution per booking without fee (~₹100)
Contribution if we keep the fee
Bookings lost to the fee-free rival
How long the rival can fund zero fees
Flight contribution per booking with fee (~₹450)
Hotel cross-sell lost with lost bookings
Waive fee for app or loyalty bookings only
Waive fee only on routes where the rival is strongest

hypotheses: Dropping the fee gives up about ₹420 crore a year (12m x ₹350); bookings would need to roughly triple to recover it, which no realistic share gain delivers.
Keeping the fee costs far less: even a 15% loss of bookings costs about ₹95 crore of contribution, including lost hotel cross-sell.
A targeted waiver for app or loyalty bookings defends the most price-sensitive repeat customers at a fraction of the cost.
hints: Compare the contribution under each pricing option, including how volume responds.
Level 1: contribution if we drop the fee, contribution if we keep it, and middle options between the two.
Middle options: a lower fee (say ₹199), a waiver for app or loyalty bookings only, or a waiver only on routes where the rival is strongest.

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per booking
keyMetrics.formula: convenience fee + airline commissions and incentives - payment and support costs

keyMetrics.name: Breakeven volume
keyMetrics.formula: current contribution / contribution per booking without the fee (including cross-sell)

commonMistakes: Assuming the client must match the rival, when the fee is about three-quarters of contribution per booking and matching costs far more than losing some share.
Ignoring hotel cross-sell entirely; it improves the no-fee case slightly but does not change the answer.

frameworkPick.why: The decision is whether to change a price, so compare contribution at each price point, including the volume response.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Profit has not yet fallen much; the question is a forward-looking price decision.
distractorWhyNot.competitive-response: The rival's move is the trigger, but the only decision asked is one price change; the rival matters only through one input (bookings lost while it keeps fees at zero), so a full competitive-response frame is wider than the question.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Dropping the fee might add bookings, but the question is whether the price change pays, not how to grow.

cases.title: Hub on-time performance has collapsed
cases.prompt: A Southeast Asian low-cost airline has seen on-time departures at its main hub fall from 85% to 72% in six months, and complaints and compensation costs are rising. The COO asks you to find out why flights are leaving late.
clarifyingFacts: Q: How is on-time defined? A: Departing within 15 minutes of the scheduled time.
Q: Did the schedule change? A: Yes. The airline added 20 daily departures at the hub and cut scheduled turnaround time from 35 to 30 minutes.
Q: Anything changing at the airport? A: A new runway is being built, and one taxiway is closed at peak hours.
Q: Is there delay data? A: Yes, each delayed flight is tagged with a delay reason by the duty manager.

modelTree.label: Why have on-time departures at the hub fallen from 85% to 72%?

children.label: Aircraft arrived late from its previous flight
Late departure from the previous airport
Longer flight or taxi-in time (holding, congestion)
Turnaround at the hub overran the 30-minute plan
Aircraft ready but held after doors closed
Air traffic control and departure slots
Pushback tug not at the aircraft when doors close

hypotheses: Cutting the planned turnaround from 35 to 30 minutes removed the buffer, so most new delays start in the turnaround and then knock on through the day.
The closed taxiway adds 5 to 10 minutes of taxi time at peaks, pushing flights already near the limit past the 15-minute threshold.
hints: Split delays along the timeline of one departure: before the aircraft lands, while it is on the ground, and after the doors close.
Level 1: aircraft arrived late, turnaround overran, aircraft held after doors closed.
Aircraft arrived late: late departure from the previous airport, and longer flight or taxi-in time (holding, congestion).

keyMetrics.name: On-time performance
keyMetrics.formula: departures within 15 minutes of schedule / total departures

keyMetrics.name: Delay minutes by cause
keyMetrics.formula: sum of delay minutes tagged to each cause code

keyMetrics.name: Turnaround buffer
keyMetrics.formula: scheduled turnaround time - median actual turnaround time

commonMistakes: Listing causes (weather, air traffic control, staff) without a timeline, so knock-on delays get double counted with the delay that caused them.
Ignoring the schedule change: a 5-minute cut in planned turnaround creates delays even if every process runs exactly as before.

frameworkPick.why: The question is why a process (departing on time) is failing, so trace the delay through the operational steps of a departure.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Compensation costs are a symptom; the question asks what causes late departures, not why profit moved.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Extra departures are one possible cause, but the client is not asking how to grow.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: Nothing suggests a financial crisis; an operating KPI has slipped, so a turnaround frame (cash, restructuring) overshoots the question.

cases.title: Launch a regional airline on UDAN routes?
cases.prompt: An Indian infrastructure group wants to launch a regional airline with 10 leased 72-seat turboprops, flying Tier-2 and Tier-3 routes under the government's UDAN scheme. It would commit about ₹600 crore over five years. Should it enter, and if so, how?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does UDAN offer? A: On awarded routes, viability gap funding (VGF) and route exclusivity for three years, in return for capped fares on about half the seats.
Q: Does the group have airline experience? A: No, but it runs three regional airports and has a strong balance sheet.
Q: What does success look like? A: Operating breakeven by year 3 and a 15% annual return on the ₹600 crore by year 5.
Q: How have past regional airlines done? A: Several have shut or shrunk after VGF ended; load factors on UDAN routes are typically 60-70%.

modelTree.label: Should the group launch a 10-turboprop UDAN airline, and how?

children.label: Travellers today by road and rail on these city pairs
Share likely to switch to air at capped fares
Exclusive UDAN routes vs contested routes
New fast trains and expressways on the same pairs
Can the group run an airline well?
Air operator certificate and DGCA safety approvals
Pilots and engineers rated on turboprops
Advantages from owning three regional airports
Time to certificate and first flight
Start-up cost of teams and systems
Price vs value of its certificate, routes and crew
Partner with a major airline (codeshare, wet lease)
Do the returns justify the risk?
Revenue: seats x load factor x fare + VGF
Cost: fuel, lease, crew, airport charges
Fare headroom above the capped level
Downside: lease commitments if routes fail

hypotheses: Most candidate routes work with VGF but need load factors above about 80% once VGF ends, well above the 60-70% typical on UDAN routes.
Owning airports helps on slots and ground costs but does not solve the binding constraints (certification, crew, safety culture), so partnering or acquiring beats building from scratch.
hints: Structure it as a go or no-go entry decision, and make the end of the subsidy visible somewhere in the structure.
Level 1: regional market attractiveness; capability to run an airline; entry route; returns.
Capability: air operator certificate and DGCA approvals; turboprop-rated pilots and engineers (availability, training pipeline); advantages from owning three regional airports.

keyMetrics.name: Revenue per flight
keyMetrics.formula: seats x load factor x average fare + VGF per flight

keyMetrics.name: Breakeven load factor
keyMetrics.formula: cost per flight / (seats x average fare)

keyMetrics.name: Payback period
keyMetrics.formula: upfront investment / annual operating cash flow

commonMistakes: Judging the market on years 1-3, when VGF and exclusivity make most routes look profitable; the real test is year 4 onwards.
Assuming that owning airports means the group can run an airline; certification, crew and safety are the binding constraints.

frameworkPick.why: The client is deciding whether and how to enter a business it is not in today, so test market attractiveness, ability to win, entry route and returns.

distractorWhyNot.growth: Growth frames assume an existing business to expand; the group has no airline today.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: This is a new business in a new industry for the client, not a new product for existing customers.
distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: The group would build and run the airline itself, not buy a company for a financial return.

cases.title: Lift ancillary revenue per passenger
cases.prompt: A European budget airline carries 40 million passengers a year at an average fare of €45 and earns about €22 of ancillary revenue per passenger on top. The board wants ancillary revenue per passenger at €30 within three years. How could it get there?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What makes up the €22 today? A: Bags about €12, seats €5, priority boarding and bundles €3, onboard sales €1.50, and third-party commissions (hotels, car hire) €0.50.
Q: Any constraints? A: Base fares should not rise, customer satisfaction scores must not fall, and passenger numbers are expected to stay roughly flat.
Q: Where do customers buy add-ons? A: About 70% of ancillary sales happen at booking, 20% in manage-booking and check-in, and 10% at the airport or onboard.
Q: How does €22 compare with rivals? A: An ultra-low-cost rival earns about €45 per passenger, mostly by charging for cabin bags and through fees at the airport.

modelTree.label: How can ancillary revenue per passenger rise from €22 to €30 in three years?

children.label: More passengers buy airline add-ons (attach rate)
Offers tailored to trip type (families, business)
Gate bag enforcement and priority upsell
Buyers spend more per airline add-on (price and mix)
Dynamic pricing of bags and seats
By route, season and days to departure
By channel (cheaper at booking than at the gate)
Mix towards bigger bags, extra legroom, premium bundles
Advertising and retail (app, boarding pass, onboard)

hypotheses: Dynamic pricing of bags and seats by route, season and booking window can add €2-3 per passenger without raising base fares.

Third-party revenue (€0.50) cannot close the gap alone: even 5% of passengers booking a hotel, car or insurance at about €20 commission adds only about €1 per passenger, so most of the €8 must come from airline add-ons.
Moving more seat and bag sales into the weeks before departure via app prompts lifts attach rates without raising headline prices.
hints: Ancillary revenue per passenger is a sum over products of attach rate x price; build the split from that identity and decide where products the airline does not sell itself belong.
Level 1: attach rate on airline add-ons; spend per buyer; third-party and new streams.
Attach rate by touchpoint: at booking (bundles, defaults), between booking and departure (app, check-in), at the airport and onboard.

keyMetrics.name: Ancillary revenue per passenger
keyMetrics.formula: sum over products of (attach rate x average price)

keyMetrics.name: Attach rate
keyMetrics.formula: passengers buying the product / total passengers

keyMetrics.name: Revenue gap
keyMetrics.formula: (€30 - €22) x 40m passengers ≈ €320m a year

commonMistakes: Copying the ultra-low-cost rival's €45 by charging for cabin bags and airport fees, which breaks the satisfaction constraint; across-the-board fee rises also ignore attach-rate levers.
Listing ideas without sizing them; each lever should be expressed in euros per passenger against the €8 gap.

frameworkPick.why: The goal is to grow a revenue line to a target, so break revenue per passenger into volume, spend and new-stream levers.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: Pricing is one lever (spend per buyer), but the question also covers attach rates and new products.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: New products are one branch; the question concerns the whole ancillary revenue line, mostly existing products.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: Profit has not fallen; the question is a revenue growth target.

cases.title: New LCC attacks our best routes
cases.prompt: Our client is a large Indian full-service airline. A newly launched low-cost airline has started flying 6 of its 10 most profitable domestic routes from Bengaluru, at fares about 25% lower. These routes bring the client about ₹1,800 crore a year, and its load factor on them has fallen from 86% to 80% in three months. How should the client respond?
clarifyingFacts: Q: How big is the entrant? A: It has 12 aircraft and plans 40 within three years, backed by a well-funded investor group.
Q: Who flies on these routes? A: About 45% of the client's passengers are business travellers, many on negotiated corporate fares; the rest travel for leisure or to visit friends and relatives.
Q: How do costs compare? A: The client's cost per seat is about 20% above the entrant's because of premium cabins, lounges and older aircraft.
Q: Any constraints? A: The client is profitable and wants to protect margins; it owns a low-cost subsidiary that flies other routes.

modelTree.label: How should the full-service airline respond to the new LCC on its 6 Bengaluru routes?

children.label: How serious and lasting is the threat?
Funding vs cash burn at launch fares
Which of our revenue is at risk?
Passengers lost so far (86% to 80% load factor)
Business travellers without a corporate contract
Which fare buckets and departures to match
Cost of matching vs passengers kept
Add flights at peak business times
Move capacity to routes without overlap
Product: sharpen the offer for business travellers
Structure: move flying to our low-cost subsidiary
Subsidiary's cost per seat vs entrant's
Revenue kept vs margin given up per option
Competition law risk of pricing below cost (CCI, if dominant)

hypotheses: Business passengers (about 45%) are largely held by contracts and schedules; the real exposure is leisure and visiting-family traffic, so a blanket fare cut gives away margin on passengers who were not leaving.
Moving the most leisure-heavy routes to the low-cost subsidiary defends share at a cost per seat close to the entrant's.
Our cost per seat is 20% above the entrant's, so its cost is only about 17% below ours, yet its fares are 25% lower; part of the discount is launch pricing that it must narrow to make money.
hints: Sequence the structure as you would brief a CEO on a rival's move: diagnosis before action.
Level 1: seriousness and duration of the threat; revenue at risk; response options; choice between options.
Threat: the entrant's cost advantage (structural versus launch-phase) and its staying power (funding against cash burn, fleet plan from 12 to 40 aircraft).

keyMetrics.name: Revenue at risk
keyMetrics.formula: passengers lost x average fare + fare reduction x passengers kept

keyMetrics.name: Cost per available seat
keyMetrics.formula: total route operating cost / seats offered

keyMetrics.name: Load factor
keyMetrics.formula: passengers carried / seats offered

commonMistakes: Matching the 25% cut on all fares, which could cost up to about ₹450 crore a year against about ₹125 crore lost from the load factor fall so far.
Ignoring the low-cost subsidiary, the one option that can match the entrant's cost base.

frameworkPick.why: A rival's move triggered the problem and the client must choose a response, weighing the entrant's staying power, its own exposure and likely counter-moves.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: Price is one response option, but capacity, product and the subsidiary matter as much.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: The cause of the revenue loss is already known (the entrant); the question is how to respond.
distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The rival is the one entering; our client is the incumbent deciding how to defend.

cases.title: Who should the new business class serve?
cases.prompt: A Middle Eastern hub airline is redesigning its long-haul business class. Premium cabins are 10% of seats but bring 30% of passenger revenue. Before spending about US$400 million on new seats and lounges, management wants to know which premium passenger segments to design for.
clarifyingFacts: Q: Who are today's premium passengers? A: About 55% fly on employer-paid tickets, 25% pay for their own tickets, and 20% are in the cabin through upgrades or points.
Q: What do they pay? A: Employer-paid tickets average about US$3,200 one-way and self-paid about US$2,400; upgrades and redemptions bring little cash.
Q: How does the hub shape the mix? A: About 70% of premium passengers connect through the hub between two other countries.
Q: What is the objective? A: Maximise premium cash revenue over the cabin's 10-year life.

modelTree.label: Which premium passenger segments should the new business class target?

children.label: Value: volume and yield per contract
Needs: schedule, flexibility, space to work and sleep
Employer-paid travellers without a corporate contract
Needs: comfort for price, easy rebooking
Needs: lounges, seats for travelling together
Needs: flexibility at a fair price
Upgraded or redeemed into the cabin (~20%)
Paid upgrades from economy or premium economy

hypotheses: Employer-paid travellers are about 55% of premium passengers but roughly three-quarters of premium cash ticket revenue, so their needs (sleep, work, schedule) should anchor the design.
Self-paid premium leisure is the growth segment and values lounges and seats for travelling together, so a layout built only for solo business travellers would under-serve it.
The 20% on upgrades and points dilutes cash yield; a smaller business cabin plus a premium economy cabin could absorb upgrades and lift revenue per seat.
hints: Segment by how the passenger came to be in the premium seat and who paid, because value and needs follow from that.
Level 1: premium ticket paid by employer, premium ticket paid by traveller, upgraded or redeemed into the cabin.
Upgraded or redeemed into the cabin: elite members upgraded on status, points redemptions, and paid upgrades from economy or premium economy.

keyMetrics.name: Segment share of cash revenue
keyMetrics.formula: segment passengers x average cash fare / total premium cash revenue

keyMetrics.name: Premium revenue per seat
keyMetrics.formula: premium cabin passenger revenue / premium seats flown

commonMistakes: Segmenting by demographics (age, nationality) rather than by who pays and why they fly, which is what drives willingness to pay and product needs.
Designing for the 70% who connect as if connection were a segment; connecting or not cuts across every payer group and shapes lounge and transfer needs, not who to design the seat for.

frameworkPick.why: Management needs to know which customer groups to design for, which means splitting premium passengers into groups with distinct value and needs and choosing targets.

distractorWhyNot.product-launch: The new cabin is a product, but the question asked is who to design it for, which comes before any launch decision.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: Fares measure segment value here, but no price is being set.
distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: The airline already knows its premium volumes; the issue is which groups matter.

cases.title: Launch a monthly flight subscription pass?
cases.prompt: An Indian low-cost airline is considering a monthly subscription for frequent business flyers: ₹14,999 a month for up to four one-way flights on one route pair, such as Mumbai-Delhi. Its frequent flyers on that route currently pay about ₹6,500 per one-way ticket on average. Should the airline launch the pass?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Who would buy it? A: Research points to SME owners and sales staff who fly the route three to five times a month.
Q: How full are the flights? A: Mumbai-Delhi runs at about 88% load factor and is close to full at morning and evening peaks.
Q: What does it cost to carry one more passenger in an empty seat? A: About ₹800 (extra fuel for the weight, passenger handling, catering, payment costs).
Q: Are the pass rules decided? A: No. The team wants your view on booking windows, blackout dates and seat limits.

modelTree.label: Should the airline launch a ₹14,999 monthly pass for four flights on a route pair?

children.label: Flying with rivals or by train today
Willingness to pay from customer research
Ticket revenue lost from customers who switch
Trips per month before the pass
Marginal cost in an otherwise empty seat (~₹800)
Fares lost when subscribers displace buyers on full flights
Seat controls: booking windows, blackouts, caps per flight
Systems: booking engine, fraud and name-change rules
How will rivals and customers react?
Customers coming to expect cheaper fares

hypotheses: Cannibalisation decides the case: each existing customer who switches cuts monthly spend from ₹26,000 to ₹14,999 (about ₹11,000 lost), while a new subscriber adds about ₹11,800, so the pass loses money if more than about half of subscribers already fly with the airline.
On peak flights near 90% full, subscribers displace last-minute buyers paying well above ₹6,500, so blackout dates or seat caps on peak departures are essential.
hints: Treat it as a launch decision and keep the economics strictly incremental: what changes only because the pass exists.
Level 1: demand; economics; ability to run it; rival and customer reaction.
Ability to run it: seat controls (booking windows, blackouts, caps per flight) and systems (booking engine, fraud and name-change rules).

keyMetrics.name: Net gain per new subscriber
keyMetrics.formula: ₹14,999 - trips used x marginal cost per seat

keyMetrics.name: Net loss per switching customer
keyMetrics.formula: previous monthly spend (trips x average fare) - ₹14,999

keyMetrics.name: Breakeven share of existing customers
keyMetrics.formula: gain per new subscriber / (gain per new subscriber + loss per switcher)

commonMistakes: Counting all pass revenue as new money, when the likeliest buyers are the airline's own most frequent, highest-paying customers.
Assuming the cost of carrying a subscriber is near zero; on a full peak flight the true cost is the fare of the passenger displaced.

frameworkPick.why: The question is whether to launch a new product, so test demand, incremental economics including cannibalisation, feasibility and reaction.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: The ₹14,999 price is one design choice inside the launch decision, not the whole question.
distractorWhyNot.growth: The pass may add volume, but the decision hinges on whether this specific product creates value.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Knowing the target customer is one input to the launch decision, not the decision itself.

cases.title: Engine groundings push LCC into crisis
cases.prompt: A mid-sized Indian low-cost airline has 60 leased aircraft, but 22 are grounded waiting for engines. It burns about ₹90 crore of cash a month, has ₹450 crore left, and lessors on 15 aircraft are demanding ₹300 crore of overdue rent. The 38 flying aircraft cover their own cash operating costs, but overheads are sized for 60. The board asks what the airline must do in the next 90 days to survive, and how it returns to profit within 18 months.
clarifyingFacts: Q: Can lessors take the aircraft back? A: Yes. Under the Cape Town Convention, which India enacted in 2025, a lessor can declare a default and ask DGCA to deregister and export the aircraft; even an insolvency filing would hold lessors off for no more than two months.

Q: What makes up the ₹90 crore monthly burn? A: Rent on the 22 grounded aircraft, about ₹3 crore each a month (about ₹66 crore); the rest is overheads that the flying fleet's contribution does not cover.
Q: What is the engine maker offering? A: About ₹15 crore per grounded aircraft per year in compensation, paid as credits against future purchases, and spare engines only from next year.
Q: Will the promoter invest? A: The promoter will put in ₹500 crore only if lessors agree to defer dues and the plan shows a path to profit; outside investors want a majority stake.

modelTree.label: What must the airline do to survive 90 days and be profitable within 18 months?

children.label: Operating cash burn (~₹90 crore a month)
Overdue rent (₹300 crore) and other arrears
Sale of owned assets (spare engines, parts)
Lessor rent deferral for lease extensions
Credit terms from fuel suppliers, airports, vendors
Decide the fate of the 22 grounded aircraft
Spare engines and shop-visit priority from the maker
Turn compensation credits into cash or rent offsets
Wet or damp lease on the most profitable routes
Cost of leased capacity vs route contribution
Cut holding costs while parked (parking, insurance, storage)
Cut routes that do not cover cash costs
Lower variable cost per flight (handling, fuel efficiency)

hypotheses: Real runway is under two months: ₹450 crore of cash less ₹300 crore of overdue rent covers only about 1.7 months of the ₹90 crore monthly burn, so a lessor standstill must come before anything else.

Rent on grounded aircraft (22 x ₹3 crore ≈ ₹66 crore a month) is about three-quarters of the burn; a rent holiday on them, traded for lease extensions and with lessors part-compensated by assigning engine-maker credits (≈ ₹27 crore a month), cuts burn to about ₹24 crore, and with the promoter's ₹500 crore gives about 27 months even after clearing the arrears.

Stakeholder goals are locked together (the promoter invests only if lessors defer, lessors defer only if new money arrives), so both must close in one package; resizing overheads to 38 aircraft then removes the last ₹24 crore.
hints: Split by time horizon, and give the root cause of the crisis its own branch rather than burying it in costs.
Level 1: fund the 90-day cash gap; decide the grounded fleet; make the flying fleet profitable.
Flying fleet: network (cut routes that do not cover cash costs, concentrate on metro routes), revenue (yield management, ancillaries) and cost (resize overheads, lower variable cost per flight).

keyMetrics.name: Cash runway (months)
keyMetrics.formula: (cash - overdue payables that must be paid now) / monthly cash burn

keyMetrics.name: Cash contribution per flying aircraft
keyMetrics.formula: route revenue - cash operating costs (fuel, crew, airport, maintenance, rent)

keyMetrics.name: Grounded share of burn
keyMetrics.formula: grounded aircraft x monthly rent / monthly cash burn (22 x ₹3 crore / ₹90 crore ≈ 73%)

commonMistakes: Jumping to long-term strategy (network, brand) before securing a lessor standstill; Cape Town remedies let lessors deregister and export aircraft quickly, and insolvency would buy at most two months.
Treating the engine maker's compensation as cash; credits against future purchases do nothing for the 90-day gap unless converted.

frameworkPick.why: The airline faces a liquidity crisis that needs a turnaround plan (cash first, then profit), and the root cause is operational: grounded aircraft that must be fixed, replaced or returned.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: A pure profit diagnosis ignores that the airline may run out of cash before any profit fix lands.
distractorWhyNot.ma: A sale may be one outcome, but the board asked how the airline survives and recovers.

cases.title: Gulf airline eyes stake in Indian carrier
cases.prompt: A large Gulf hub airline is considering buying 49% of a mid-sized Indian airline for about ₹2,500 crore. The Indian airline has 40 aircraft, about 8% domestic share, ₹8,000 crore of revenue and a small operating loss. The Gulf airline wants Indian traffic to feed its hub, the Indian promoter wants growth capital and to keep control, and Indian rivals are expected to lobby against the deal. Should the Gulf airline do it?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What do the rules allow? A: Foreign airlines may own up to 49% of an Indian scheduled airline (FDI and portfolio investment combined) with government approval; substantial ownership and effective control must stay with Indian nationals, and the chairman and at least two-thirds of directors must be Indian citizens.

Q: Can the Gulf airline simply add its own flights to India? A: No. Its seats under the bilateral air services agreement are fully used and India has shown no sign of raising them. Indian-side seats are allocated by the government among Indian airlines, so the partner would need a larger allocation to add flights to the hub.

Q: What synergies does the Gulf airline expect? A: About ₹1,200 crore a year of extra revenue on its own network from Indian connecting passengers, at roughly 25% contribution (pre-tax), plus procurement and maintenance savings it has not quantified. Assume synergies last 10 years and a 12% discount rate.
Q: What is the Indian airline worth on its own? A: Assume about ₹2,000 crore of equity value on its own plan.

modelTree.label: Should the Gulf airline buy 49% of the Indian airline for ₹2,500 crore?

children.label: Is the stake worth the price on a standalone basis?
Path from small loss to profit
Cost per seat vs larger Indian rivals
Share and yield trend in a concentrated market
Implied ₹5,100 crore equity value vs ~₹2,000 crore standalone
Lease liabilities and capital needed to grow
What synergies can the Gulf airline actually capture?
Revenue: Indian passengers fed to the hub
Partner flights to the hub on Indian-side seat allocations
Codeshare and joint sales on domestic feed
Dis-synergies: partner's own international plans vs hub feed
Can the deal be approved and governed?
Government stance on bilateral rights feeding a foreign hub
Board seats, vetoes and management rights
Is there a better route into India?
Codeshare or revenue-sharing joint venture without equity
Stake in a different Indian airline
Wait and push for a larger bilateral

hypotheses: Most of the deal's value depends on the partner winning Indian-side seats to fly to the Gulf hub; if the government withholds them, synergies shrink to codeshare level and the price cannot be justified.
The partners' goals conflict: the promoter wants capital for domestic and wider international growth, while the Gulf airline wants the partner's international flying pointed at its hub.

The price is about ₹1,500 crore above the stake's standalone value (₹2,500 crore vs 49% of ₹2,000 crore); ₹300 crore a year of synergy contribution for 10 years at 12% is worth about ₹1,700 crore, so the deal pays only if close to 90% of the network synergies are delivered.
hints: Value the stake as any acquirer would, then ask what a strategic buyer must add in a market where traffic rights and control are regulated.
Level 1: standalone value; synergies that can actually be captured; approval and governance; alternatives.
Alternatives: a codeshare or revenue-sharing joint venture without equity, a stake in a different Indian airline, or waiting and pushing for a larger bilateral.

keyMetrics.name: Implied equity value
keyMetrics.formula: price paid / stake acquired (₹2,500 crore / 49% ≈ ₹5,100 crore)

keyMetrics.name: Synergy capture needed to break even
keyMetrics.formula: (price - 49% x standalone equity value) / PV of synergies (₹1,500 crore / ₹1,695 crore ≈ 88%)

keyMetrics.name: Synergy contribution
keyMetrics.formula: extra network revenue x contribution margin (₹1,200 crore x ~25% ≈ ₹300 crore a year)

commonMistakes: Treating synergies as certain when they depend on the government letting Indian bilateral rights feed a foreign hub.
Ignoring that a 49% stake with Indian effective control means the Gulf airline cannot direct the network; governance rights matter as much as price.

frameworkPick.why: This is an acquisition decision (value, synergies, price, governance) and also the Gulf airline's chosen route into a market it cannot grow in on its own, so other entry routes must be compared.

distractorWhyNot.growth: Growth is the motive, but the question is whether this specific acquisition is the right way to achieve it.
distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: The buyer is a strategic acquirer seeking network synergies, not a financial investor seeking an exit return.

cases.title: PE fund weighs European ground handler
cases.prompt: A private equity fund is considering buying an independent ground-handling company that serves airlines at 12 European airports. It has €600 million of revenue and €54 million of EBITDA, and the seller wants 9x EBITDA. Air traffic is growing about 3% a year, and the fund needs 2.5x its equity in five years. Should it buy?
clarifyingFacts: Q: How is the deal financed? A: About 4x EBITDA of debt (€216 million) and €270 million of fund equity, ignoring fees. Assume exit after five years at the same 9x, with net debt cut to about €120 million from cash flow.

Q: How does the company win work? A: Under EU rules, airports above about 2 million passengers a year may limit ramp and baggage handlers (to no fewer than two) and award those licences by tender for up to seven years; licences at two airports, about 35% of revenue, are re-tendered within two years.
Q: What drives costs? A: Staff are about 65% of costs, and a new collective agreement raises wages 5% next year.
Q: How are airline contracts priced? A: Mostly per aircraft turn, on three to five year terms; only some include inflation indexation.

modelTree.label: Should the fund buy the ground handler at 9x EBITDA (€486 million)?

children.label: Traffic growth at its 12 airports (~3% a year)
Growth plans of its main airline customers
Licence limits and tender cycles at large airports
Chance of keeping the two licences re-tendered (35% of revenue)
Labour productivity: staff hours per turn
Wage inflation: 5% rise next year on 65% of costs
Service quality: on-time turns and baggage performance
Can EBITDA grow from €54 million to about €90 million?
New airports, contracts and services (cargo, de-icing)
Downside returns if one re-tendered licence is lost

hypotheses: Traffic growth is not the value driver: with staff at 65% of costs, the 5% wage rise adds about €18 million of cost, a third of EBITDA, unless contracts pass it through.
Reaching about €90 million of EBITDA needs roughly 10% growth a year, so margin must rise from 9% to about 12-13% even if every licence is retained.

Losing one re-tendered licence (about 17.5% of revenue) caps year-5 EBITDA near €73 million even at a 12.7% margin, about 2.0x equity, so the price should reflect re-tender risk or include an earn-out.
hints: Use the due-diligence sequence a fund follows, then work back from the 2.5x target to the EBITDA needed at exit.
Level 1: market attractiveness; defensibility of licences, contracts and costs; EBITDA growth plan; deal returns and downside.
Market: volume growth (traffic at its 12 airports, main airline customers' plans) and market structure (licence limits and tender cycles, airline self-handling and rival handlers).

keyMetrics.name: Equity multiple
keyMetrics.formula: (exit EBITDA x exit multiple - net debt at exit) / equity invested

keyMetrics.name: Required exit EBITDA
keyMetrics.formula: (2.5 x €270m + net debt at exit) / exit multiple ≈ €88m at 9x with ~€120m net debt

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per aircraft turn
keyMetrics.formula: revenue per turn - staff and equipment cost per turn

commonMistakes: Resting the investment case on traffic growth; in a labour-heavy business with partial indexation, wages can outrun volume.
Treating licences as permanent; EU tender cycles mean a third of revenue can be lost within the holding period.

frameworkPick.why: A financial buyer must test market, target and deal returns, and here the return depends on operational levers (rostering, productivity, passing through wage costs) in a labour-heavy business.

distractorWhyNot.ma: M&A frames centre on synergies with the buyer's own business; a PE fund has none and needs a standalone return.
distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The fund is buying a company for a return on exit, not entering a market to operate in for the long term.

children.label: Deplaning (steps or airbridge in place, doors open)

Ground-time cost per minute (lease, crew, parking)

flaws.explanation: Refuelling is missing from aircraft servicing. On a narrowbody turn it is often on the critical path, and where fuelling with passengers on board needs extra safety steps it can hold up boarding.
The cost of each minute on the ground tells you what the extra 15 minutes cost; it does not make the turnaround any slower, so it is a consequence, not a driver.
flaws.fix: Remove it from the tree; use it later when sizing the value of fixing the problem.

decoys.whyFine: The load and trim sheet can only be closed once final passenger and bag numbers are known, so its sign-off is a genuine step on the critical path.

tree.label: How can an Indian OTA grow revenue from domestic flight bookings?

children.label: Get existing customers to book more often
Add-ons sold with the booking (insurance, seats, meals)

flaws.explanation: Re-engaging lapsed users is one tactic for getting existing customers to book more often, yet it sits at the same level as the two top-level revenue drivers.
flaws.fix: Move it under 'Get existing customers to book more often' as one tactic.

flaws.explanation: Take rate is simply airline commissions, incentives and customer fees expressed as a share of ticket value, so it is the same money as b1 and b2 in different wording, counted twice.
flaws.fix: Delete it; if take rate is the preferred lens, use it instead of b1 and b2, not alongside them.

decoys.whyFine: Insurance, seats and meals sold with a flight booking are revenue the OTA earns per flight booking, so they belong in revenue per booking.

children.label: Leisure and other personal travellers at risk
Match fares in our lowest fare buckets

flaws.fix: Merge into one pricing option, e.g. 'Price: match or undercut selectively in lower fare buckets on contested routes'.

Overlap: currency cuts across the fixed and variable buckets; leases and much of fuel and maintenance are dollar-linked, so they would be counted twice.
Overlap: power-by-the-hour contracts are how much of the engine maintenance bill is paid, so that cost already sits in maintenance.

Gap: profit = ASKs x (RASK - CASK), so a change in capacity moves profit even when unit revenue and unit cost are flat.
Operating profit = ASKs x (RASK - CASK). Taking capacity at last year's unit margin, then RASK and CASK changes at this year's capacity, the three effects add up exactly to the change in profit.

quick.question: Which split of 'Fuel cost per ASK of an Indian airline' is MECE?
quick.parent: Fuel cost per ASK of an Indian airline

split: Jet fuel price per litre in dollars
options.why: Gap: the rupee-dollar exchange rate is missing; jet fuel is priced off dollar benchmarks, so a weaker rupee raises fuel cost even with flat dollar prices and flat VAT.

Fuel cost per ASK is exactly rupee price per litre times litres per ASK; benchmark price, exchange rate, taxes and into-plane fees sit in the first, fleet, sector length and flying practice in the second.
Overlap: the rupee price already reflects the exchange rate, so depreciation is counted twice.
Not a driver: more flights raise total fuel cost but not fuel cost per ASK.

chainDrills.prompt: Monthly rentals for new narrowbody aircraft rise about 15% because manufacturers cannot deliver aircraft fast enough. In which stage does this cost originate?
chainDrills.why: Lease rentals are set by lessors and by the supply of new aircraft, both in the aircraft, engines and leasing stage. The airline (s4) pays the higher rent, but the cause is upstream scarcity.

chainDrills.prompt: Put the stages in order, from the aircraft as an asset (built, financed, then kept airworthy), through the inputs each flight consumes, to the airline and on to the end traveller.
chainDrills.why: Aircraft are built and financed (s1) and kept airworthy by MRO (s2); airports, fuel and ground services (s3) are the infrastructure each flight needs; the airline plans and flies the network (s4); distribution sells the seats (s5); and ancillaries and loyalty earn more from the traveller (s6).

chainDrills.prompt: An Indian full-service airline's distribution cost per passenger rises because more corporate bookings now come through agents using a GDS, which charges the airline a fee for each flight segment booked. Which stage earns this fee?
chainDrills.why: GDS segment fees are revenue for the distribution stage. The airline bears the cost, but the pricing power sits with the GDS, which is why airlines push direct and NDC bookings.

chainDrills.prompt: Assign each item to the stage whose business earns it as revenue or, for a metric, the stage it measures.

items.item: Monthly rental on a leased A320neo
Engine shop visit after a set number of flight cycles
User development fee (UDF) shown on the passenger's ticket
Load factor on the Delhi-Mumbai route
Fee per flight segment charged by a GDS
Points bought by a bank for its co-brand credit card

chainDrills.why: The UDF appears on the airline ticket, but it is airport revenue (s3); the airline only collects and passes it on. The lease rental is the airline's biggest fixed cost but is earned by the lessor (s1). Points sold to a bank are loyalty revenue (s6) even if the cardholder never flies.

chainDrills.prompt: A full-service airline's operating margin is unchanged, but its cash balance jumps by about ₹1,500 crore after a bank partner pays upfront for several years of points for its co-brand card. In which stage is this value created?
chainDrills.why: Pre-sold points are a loyalty transaction: the bank pays cash now, and the airline books deferred revenue that it recognises as points are redeemed or expire. The value sits in s6, not in flight operations, which is why loyalty programmes can fund airlines through a crisis.

chainDrills.prompt: After a terminal expansion, the regulator approves sharply higher landing and user development charges at a metro airport. The airline's cost per ASK rises 2% and its all-in fares lose ground to rail. Where does the root cause sit?
chainDrills.why: The cost shows up in the airline's CASK (s4), but it originates in regulated airport charges (s3), which AERA sets to give the airport its allowed return on the new terminal investment.
